title: Cognitive Architecture
authors: Ann Sussman and Justin B. Hollander, 2021
central_proposition: Understanding human beings as products of Darwinian evolution, with built-in responses to the environment, is crucial for architects and planners to design and plan more creatively and successfully.

concept_definitions.name: Evolution
concept_definitions.definition: All life evolved, or transformed, from a common ancestor, including modern humans who carry significant 'baggage' from a long evolutionary journey.

concept_definitions.name: Natural Selection
concept_definitions.definition: The mechanism explaining how transformation happens and why diverse species exist, where individuals with profitable variations have a better chance of surviving and propagating their modified form.

concept_definitions.name: Cognitive Architecture
concept_definitions.definition: The exploration of how research in psychology and the cognitive sciences can inform the understanding of the impact of buildings and city design on people.

concept_definitions.name: Thigmotaxis
concept_definitions.definition: A survival and orientation strategy, observed across diverse species including humans, where individuals tend to stick to the sides of spaces rather than open centers.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia Hypothesis
concept_definitions.definition: An innate bond between humans and all other living things, leading to a preference for natural scenes and savanna-like views.

argument_structure: The book introduces the core idea that human nature is fundamentally biological and evolved. It then dedicates subsequent chapters to specific 'hidden aspects' of human nature—unconscious tendencies and behaviors—such as thigmotaxis, visual prioritization of faces, preference for symmetry and curves, the human need for narrative, and biophilia. Each chapter outlines the evolutionary basis and implications of these traits for architectural and urban design, culminating in a discussion of biometric tools for evidence-based design and a re-evaluation of modern architectural history.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Human perceptual systems and aesthetic preferences are not arbitrary but are 'at root biological,' having evolved over millennia to register aspects of the external world critical for survival in the natural environment. These innate, often unconscious, responses to environmental stimuli (e.g., edges, patterns, symmetry, nature) drive human behavior, emotional attachments, and cognitive processes in the built world. Design that aligns with these evolved mechanisms will be more successful and resonate more deeply with human experience.

findings.antecedent: Understanding human beings as an artifact of Darwin's theory of evolution
findings.consequent: Ability to design and plan for them
findings.mechanism: Evolution has shaped human perceptual systems and aesthetic sense to prioritize survival-relevant environmental features, and aligning design with these innate responses will lead to more successful outcomes.
findings.quote: The thesis of this book is that the more we understand how human beings are an artifact of Darwin's theory of evolution, the more creatively and successfully we will be able to design and plan for them.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited research in evolutionary biology, psychology, neuroscience, genetics.

findings.consequent: Registration of external world aspects important for survival
findings.mechanism: Our species evolved in the natural world, not man-made, leading to innate responses and expectations that are still present today.
findings.quote: "Our perceptual systems are designed to register aspects of the external world that were important to our survival ..."
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited Steven Pinker (2003) on perceptual systems.

findings.antecedent: Unconscious human tendencies and behaviors (e.g., thigmotaxis, face prioritization, symmetry preference, narrative seeking, biophilia)
findings.mechanism: These hidden, evolutionarily conserved traits, often operating outside conscious control, profoundly influence how humans perceive, interact with, and form attachments to architectural and urban spaces.
findings.quote: people have multiple unconscious tendencies and behaviors that govern their responses to built environments
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited research on thigmotaxis, face processing, psychological preferences.

findings.antecedent: Environmental features (e.g., edges, sides of streets)
findings.mechanism: The 'wall-hugging' trait (thigmotaxis), an ancient survival strategy, causes people to avoid open centers and stick to edges, influencing walkability and spatial use.
findings.quote: people avoid the center of open spaces and tend to stick to the sides of streets, even in car-free zones.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited Jane Jacobs' observations, psychological research on thigmotaxis in various species.

findings.antecedent: Visual information (e.g., building elevations, urban layout)
findings.mechanism: The human brain is primarily oriented toward vision, dedicating significant gray matter to visual processing, and innately prioritizes faces for rapid identification, leading to pareidolia and emotional attachment to 'face-like' architectural elements.
findings.quote: More of our gray matter is devoted to creating our visual representation of the world than anything else... our mental apparatus does not handle visual inputs equally either—it prioritizes the face.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited neuroscientific findings on visual processing primacy, research on pareidolia.

findings.antecedent: Bilateral symmetry and curvilinear shapes in design
findings.consequent: Human aesthetic preference and psychological response
findings.mechanism: Bilateral symmetry, common in animals, is innately associated with power and robustness due to natural selection, and humans consistently prefer symmetrical faces and patterns. Curves are also innately preferred, contributing to positive aesthetic judgments.
findings.quote: animals and humans consistently associate the shape with power and robustness... they consistently preferred the more symmetrical.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited psychological research on symmetric preferences.

findings.antecedent: Settings that engage storytelling behavior (e.g., buildings with 'embedded narrative', specific formal sequences)
findings.mechanism: Humans possess complex neural circuitry for narrative invention and seeking, an adaptive trait that leads to emotional attachment and memory formation in places that offer a 'story' or a clear sequence (beginning, middle, end).
findings.quote: people love settings that engage their storytelling behavior... Many of the world's most famous buildings, sites, and cities also possess 'embedded narrative.'
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited popularity of narrative media (books, movies), Disneyland's success, Villa Lante garden design.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to nature and natural landscapes (e.g., savanna-like views, biophilic design elements)
findings.consequent: Human preference, well-being, and stress recovery
findings.mechanism: The 'biophilia hypothesis' posits an innate human bond with living things, stemming from our evolutionary history in savanna environments. This predisposition leads to a statistical gravitation towards nature, which supports psychological restoration and reduces stress.
findings.quote: people like looking at nature and seeing landscapes that recall their species-specific past... Our 'urge to affiliate with other forms of life is to some degree innate.'
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited E.O. Wilson's biophilia hypothesis, research on savanna preference.

findings.consequent: Understanding of architectural experience and human responses
findings.mechanism: Biometric tools allow observation of hidden, unconscious, and rapid human responses to the built environment, providing empirical data for evidence-based design that accounts for our evolutionary traits.
findings.quote: reviews key biometric tools that allow us to see our hidden evolutionary traits at work.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Implied by the existence of Chapter 7, which reviews these tools.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Architectural designs that incorporate elements appealing to innate human preferences (e.g., edges for thigmotaxis, face-like patterns, bilateral symmetry, narrative sequences, natural views) will elicit more positive implicit emotional responses and engagement than designs that do not.

The use of biometric tools like eye-tracking will reveal consistent, unconscious visual prioritization of specific architectural features (e.g., faces, symmetrical elements, natural patterns) across diverse human populations, regardless of explicit aesthetic judgments.

Urban planning that creates walkable places by providing clear edges and varied visual stimuli, catering to thigmotaxis and visual primacy, will lead to increased pedestrian activity and perceived comfort compared to open, undifferentiated spaces.

Exposure to biophilic design elements will lead to measurable physiological stress reduction (e.g., lower cortisol, improved HRV) and enhanced self-reported well-being compared to environments lacking such elements.
bridge_warrants: The book bridges the arts and sciences by applying findings from evolutionary biology, psychology, and neuroscience to the fields of architecture and urban planning.
It connects Jane Jacobs' observations about human behavior in cities to scientific concepts like thigmotaxis, providing a biological basis for her intuitions.
The framework integrates cognitive science (e.g., visual processing, narrative cognition) with design principles to create more human-centered environments.
model_structure: The proposed framework posits that human responses to the built environment are governed by a hierarchy of evolved biological mechanisms. These mechanisms, shaped by natural selection in the natural world, manifest as unconscious tendencies and preferences. The book's structure reflects this by dedicating chapters to specific, fundamental human traits (thigmotaxis, face perception, symmetry, narrative, biophilia) and then discussing how these can be empirically measured (biometrics) and used to re-interpret architectural history. The model implies a 'bottom-up' influence of biology on design effectiveness.
limitations: The book acknowledges a central paradox: humans evolved in the natural world, not man-made, and therefore our innate responses are not perfectly adapted to contemporary built environments.

It implicitly acknowledges the complexity of human behavior, noting that unconscious traits are 'hard to see' and were 'not well documented' in the past, suggesting the need for new tools and approaches.
